title: CCBHCs and prospective payment
one_liner: A clinic model paid a daily rate for a required set of services, and why Alabama is converting to it.
why_here: Section 12 calls the CCBHC transition the largest change in how community mental health care is paid for in a generation, and Domains 2 and 3 lean on it whenever they discuss hand-offs between services. The argument depends on seeing how a daily rate differs from a fee per service.

further_reading.title: National Council for Mental Wellbeing, What Is a CCBHC?
Alabama Department of Mental Health, Office of Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinics
ADMH, CCBHC Demonstration Billing Manual, version 3 (1 July 2026)

self_check.q: A care coordinator at a CCBHC spends a morning on the phone arranging a client's discharge from hospital. The client is not seen by the clinic that day. How is that morning paid for under Alabama's daily rate?
options: Medicaid pays the clinic a separate fee for each phone call the coordinator makes.
It triggers the full daily payment for that client, just as a therapy session would.
It is unpaid, exactly as it would be under fee-for-service, and the clinic absorbs the cost.
It triggers no payment that day, but coordination costs are built into the rate earned when clients are seen.
self_check.explanation: Care coordination is an allowable cost in the clinic's cost report. It raises the daily rate without itself triggering a payment.

self_check.q: A CCBHC must serve anyone who comes, whether or not they can pay. Why does the report say the model still leaves Alabama's uninsured adults as a financing problem?
options: Because CCBHCs are allowed to turn away people who have no insurance and cannot pay.
Because the daily rate is paid only for people enrolled in Medicaid, so care for the uninsured needs other money.
Because the federal block grant already pays in full for uninsured adults at every clinic.
Because the daily rate is set lower for uninsured clients than for Medicaid enrollees.
self_check.explanation: The obligation to serve is universal; the payment is not. In a state that has not expanded Medicaid, that gap falls back on state funds.

self_check.q: A clinic's costs turn out to be higher than its cost report predicted. Under a prospective payment system, what happens?
options: It goes on receiving the rate fixed in advance until the rate is recalculated on its actual costs.
It bills Medicaid for the difference at the end of each month, and is paid in arrears.
Its clients are charged the difference through a sliding fee added to each visit.
It loses its certification and returns to fee-for-service payment the next quarter.
self_check.explanation: 'Prospective' means set ahead of time. Alabama re-bases each clinic's rate on actual cost and visit data after its second demonstration year.

body: Most people assume a clinic is paid for what it does, one item at a time. A therapy session has a price, a medication visit has another, and the clinic sends a bill for each. That is
: a set amount per procedure code, from the Agency's published schedule

The trouble lies in what has no code. Nobody bills for ringing a client who missed an appointment, or for the hour spent finding a bed, or for keeping a crisis worker awake at three in the morning in case the phone rings. Work that earns nothing tends not to get done. So a system paid by the item ends up with plenty of items and very little joining them together. Alabama's own
manual makes the point from the other side when it lists care coordination as an activity that triggers no payment by itself
The Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic, or CCBHC, is a federal answer to that. It has two halves. The first is a list of obligations. A CCBHC must provide nine kinds of service, among them
treatment for mental illness and substance use, round-the-clock crisis response, primary-care screening,
, and it must serve anyone who comes, "regardless of their place of residence, ability to pay, or age"
The second half is the payment. A clinic adds up what it costs in a year to run everything on the list, coordination and crisis cover included, and files that as a
. Dividing the total by the clinic's daily visits gives a rate for that clinic alone
. The rate is "prospective" because it is fixed ahead of time. Alabama uses the daily version, known as
, under which the clinic receives "a single payment each day when at least one CCBHC triggering event service is provided to a Medicaid enrollee"
. One visit or four on the same day, the payment is the same.
The key idea in one picture

Draw two panels side by side. The left panel is headed "Fee-for-service". It shows two small boxes, "therapy session" and "medication visit", each with an arrow to a box marked "payment per procedure code"

, and a third box, "care coordination and follow-up", with no arrow. The right panel is headed "Prospective daily rate (PPS-1)". At the top a wide box reads "total yearly cost of operating the clinic: triggering services plus allowable activities such as care coordination". An arrow labelled "cost report, divided by daily visits" leads down to "clinic-specific daily rate". A second arrow runs from a box reading "a day on which a Medicaid enrollee receives at least one triggering service" to "one daily payment"
. A curved arrow from "daily rate" back to the top box is labelled "re-based on actual costs after the second year"
, and on 4 June 2024 Alabama was named one of ten states added to it
. Only a community mental health center designated by the Department may apply, which keeps the model inside the existing network of 19 centers
. A clinic may contract some of the nine services out to partner organizations, though it must deliver at least 51 percent of encounters itself
Conversion is happening a few centers at a time. WellStone in Huntsville and AltaPointe in Mobile were certified from July 2024
. Mountain Lakes received federal approval in October 2025 and Highland Health Systems in April 2026
. The Department's own directory lists a fifth clinic that its May 2026 announcement does not name
, and six more providers received grants in August 2026 to prepare
. The Department describes its aim as a statewide transformation

The details of what triggers a payment say a good deal about the model's intent. A visit with a certified peer specialist is enough to trigger the daily rate. Case management does not trigger it but is carried as a cost inside it
Early evidence is thin and encouraging. The first two clinics served 30,275 people in
. At WellStone the wait for an initial evaluation fell from 18 days in January 2025 to less than one day in December 2025, by the Department's account
. No clinical outcome measures, such as hospital or emergency-room use, were found in the Department's published reports as of October 2026.
There is one firm limit. The daily rate is paid for Medicaid enrollees
. A CCBHC must still see the uninsured, and in a state that has not
there are many of them, but the rate does not pay for their care.
Section 12 sets out the model and names the clinics. Read it beside Domain 2, where the crisis services are shown living on
lines that the Legislature can cut or attach conditions to

. The report's argument is that a CCBHC moves some of that work, for people with Medicaid, inside a payment the clinic earns in the ordinary way. Domain 3 makes the companion point about hand-offs: when one clinic is paid for crisis response, outpatient care and follow-up together, the gaps between them become that clinic's problem
Keep two cautions in mind as you read. The phrase "all 19 centers will convert" appears in no Department source, and the report avoids it
. And a center that has received a preparation grant is not yet a CCBHC.

title: Civil commitment
one_liner: How a person can be ordered into mental health treatment in Alabama: who asks, who decides, on what proof, for how long, and into which beds.
why_here: Domain 1 lists civil commitment among the legal foundations of the system, Section 10 places it at Intercept 2, and the long argument over 'civil-commitment beds' in Domains 2, 3 and 5 is about where committed people can be sent.

further_reading.title: Code of Alabama, Title 22, Chapter 52, Article 1: civil commitment (contents)
Code of Alabama §22-52-10.4: findings necessary for inpatient treatment
Code of Alabama §22-52-10.2: findings necessary for outpatient treatment
Code of Alabama §22-52-7: limits on liberty before the hearing

self_check.q: A physician believes a patient is dangerously ill and should be hospitalized against his will. Under Alabama's commitment law, who makes that decision?
options: The physician, by signing an involuntary admission order at the hospital where the patient is seen.
The Department of Mental Health, once it has confirmed that a bed is free in a state hospital.
The sheriff of the county where the patient lives, on the advice of the community mental health center.
A probate judge, after a sworn petition and a hearing; the physician may file the petition.
self_check.explanation: Commitment in Alabama is a court proceeding. Medical opinion is evidence in it, and the judge decides.

self_check.q: The statute tells the judge to order 'the least restrictive alternative necessary and available'. Why does the word 'available' carry so much weight in practice?
options: Because a judge can choose only among options that exist; where community care is thin, that may mean a hospital bed or nothing.
Because it lets a judge order any hospital in the state to add beds for people the court commits.
Because it means commitment is allowed only when a family member is available to supervise the person.
Because it requires the respondent to be available in person at both the probable-cause and final hearings.
self_check.explanation: The principle favours the mildest setting that will work, but it cannot conjure a service. The statute also says providers need not expand services without funding.

self_check.q: A man with a long-standing psychotic illness repeatedly drops out of treatment and gets worse, but has threatened no one and is not harming himself. Which order does the statute leave open?
options: Inpatient commitment, because deterioration without treatment is enough by itself to meet the inpatient test.
Outpatient commitment, if a designated facility consents; that test turns on deterioration and dropping out of care.
No order of any kind, because every form of commitment requires a real and present threat of harm.
A criminal competency evaluation, because refusing treatment places him under the forensic system.
self_check.explanation: The inpatient test requires a real and present threat of substantial harm. The outpatient test does not, though the treating facility has to consent.

body: is treatment ordered by a court for a person who has not agreed to it and has not been charged with a crime. Most people imagine it as a medical decision: a doctor in an emergency room signs a form and the patient is admitted. In Alabama it is a court case, heard by a
It begins with a petition. Any individual may file one, in the probate court of the county where the person is

. Probate courts are the county courts most people know from wills and estates. The petition has to be sworn, and it has to describe the specific behavior that makes the petitioner believe the person is mentally ill
The judge then appoints a guardian ad litem to protect the rights of the person named, who is called the respondent

. If the petition asks for the respondent to be held before the hearing, the judge may allow that only to prevent a real and present threat of harm or to stop the person leaving the court's reach. Even then the law is firm on one point: "No respondent shall be placed in a jail or other facility for individuals accused of or convicted of committing crimes"
. A probable-cause hearing must follow within seven days, and the final hearing within 30 days of the petition being served
At the final hearing the test is strict. The judge needs

, a standard that sits between the ordinary civil one and the criminal one. For an inpatient order four things must be shown. The person has a mental illness. Because of it he or she poses a real and present threat of substantial harm to self or others. Without treatment the person will go on deteriorating. And the person cannot make a rational decision about treatment
The key idea in one picture
Draw a timeline running left to right with five stations. Station 1: "Petition: sworn, filed by any person in the county probate court"

. Station 2: "Judge appoints a guardian ad litem". A side branch drops from Station 2 to a box, "Temporary limits on liberty: only to prevent harm or flight; never in a jail", and an arrow from that box rejoins the line at Station 3, "Probable-cause hearing within 7 days"
. Station 4: "Final hearing within 30 days of service; proof by clear and convincing evidence". Station 5 splits into three outcomes: "Petition dismissed"; "
order, up to 150 days, only if a designated facility consents"; "Inpatient order, up to 150 days, renewable for up to one year"
. Over the two commitment outcomes write "
Once the test is met, the judge does not have a free hand. The statute says the order must be for the least restrictive alternative that is "necessary and available"

, where the person lives at home under an order to accept treatment. The outpatient test is different from the inpatient one. It does not require a threat of harm. The judge has to find that the person will deteriorate without treatment and "is unable to maintain consistent engagement with outpatient treatment on a voluntary basis"
. There is a catch. Outpatient treatment can be ordered only if the designated facility has consented to provide it
Either kind of order lasts at most 150 days. A renewal can run for up to a year
The word "available" is where the law meets the budget. An inpatient order sends the person to the
or in a facility the Department designates
. In January 2026 the Department counted 771 such beds: 285 at Bryce and Harper hospitals, 234 contracted in community hospitals, and 252
residents. The benchmark the Department uses, taken from the Treatment Advocacy Center, is 30 per 100,000, or 1,550 beds
. An order does not create a bed, and the statute says as much: nothing in it requires "a mental health provider to expand his or her current services if necessary funding is not provided"
So "civil-commitment beds" has become a budget line. The
carries $8 million for civil commitment and
and a further $2.5 million for additional beds
. The Department prices closing the 779-bed gap at $226.4 million as a
. One number is missing. Alabama publishes how many beds it has for committed people, but no annual count of commitments was found in the Department's reports as of October 2026.
Domain 1 sets out the law in a paragraph, and Section 10 returns to it at

2, where a probate petition is one of the routes by which a person in crisis ends up before a judge. Domain 3 and Domain 5 carry the bed counts. When those domains say "involuntary beds" or "civil beds", they mean beds that can receive a person under a probate order, as distinct from the
Probate judges appear elsewhere in the report as partners of the mental health system. A 2025 law gives a probate judge a place on the executive committee of the larger
. For a local advocate that matters, because the county probate court is where commitment orders are made and the state publishes no count of them.

title: Competency and forensic care
one_liner: What happens when a defendant is too ill to stand trial, why people wait in Alabama jails for a hospital bed, and the two federal cases that govern care in custody.
why_here: Domain 3 and Section 10 treat the forensic waitlist as the system's most urgent failure, and Domain 1 counts the Hunter and Braggs cases among the legal foundations of the whole system. The two cases are easy to confuse and concern different people and different agencies.

further_reading.title: Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse, Hunter v. Boswell (case summary)
Alabama Rules of Criminal Procedure, Rule 11.1: definition of incompetency
ADMH Office of Forensic Mental Health Services, Overview of Forensic Mental Health Services
Southern Poverty Law Center, Braggs, et al. v. Lovelace, et al. (case page)

self_check.q: A court is told that a defendant has been 'restored to competency'. What has changed?
options: He has been found not guilty because of his mental illness.
He has recovered from his illness and no longer needs treatment.
He is now able to understand the proceedings and work with his lawyer, so the criminal case can go ahead.
He has been transferred from the Department of Corrections to the Department of Mental Health.
self_check.explanation: Competency is about present ability to take part in a trial. Restoration is a legal threshold, and a person can cross it while still seriously ill.

self_check.q: The forensic waitlist fell from 327 people in January 2026 to 291 in July. What can that number not tell you?
options: How long the people on the list have been waiting.
Whether the list was longer or shorter than six months earlier.
Roughly how many people were in jail awaiting competency services in July.
Whether the Department had reached its goal of 100.
self_check.explanation: The waitlist is a count on a given day. A shorter list can still contain people who have waited more than a year, which is what the consent decree's deadlines are about.

self_check.q: Hunter and Braggs are both federal cases about mental health care for people in custody in Alabama. What separates them?
options: Hunter is about juveniles held by the Department of Youth Services and Braggs is about adults in county jails.
Hunter covers people in county jails awaiting competency services from the Department of Mental Health; Braggs covers people in state prisons.
Hunter is a state-court case under Alabama's commitment law and Braggs is a federal constitutional case.
Hunter ended in 2003 and Braggs was filed to replace it when federal court supervision lapsed.
self_check.explanation: They involve different people at different stages and different agencies. The case that ended in 2003 was Wyatt, about patients in state hospitals.

body: " simply means connected with the courts. Forensic mental health care is care for people who are in the criminal justice system, and most of it concerns one question: is this defendant able to stand trial? In Alabama an office of the

A trial is only fair if the accused can take part in it. Alabama's court rules say a defendant is incompetent if he or she "lacks sufficient present ability to assist in his or her defense by consulting with counsel with a reasonable degree of rational understanding"
is about the defendant's state of mind now, in the courtroom. Whether illness explains what the person did at the time of the alleged offense is a separate question, with a separate evaluation

When there is enough doubt, the court orders an evaluation. If the judge then finds the defendant incompetent, and there is a substantial probability that treatment will change that within a reasonable time, the defendant is committed to the Department of Mental Health for what is called

. Restoration is a legal goal. It aims to get the person well enough to understand the proceedings and work with a lawyer, which is not the same as recovery. Until it happens the case generally cannot move
The key idea in one picture

Draw a flowchart running left to right. Box 1: "Defendant charged; held in county jail". Box 2: "Doubt about competency; court orders evaluation". Box 3, a diamond: "Competent?" A "yes" arrow leads to "Case proceeds". A "no" arrow leads to Box 4: "Court commits defendant to the Department of Mental Health for restoration"
. Between Box 4 and Box 5 insert a shaded box: "
: waiting in county jail for a bed (291 people, July 2026)"
program in the jail". An arrow from Box 5 returns to "Case proceeds", labelled "restored". Under the arrow into Box 3 write "
: 60 days"; under the arrow into Box 5 write "consent decree: 30 days", with a footnote that these are the terms as the Associated Press describes them
. In a separate panel, drawn apart, put one box: "
: people serving sentences in state prisons (
)", labelled "a different case and a different agency".

You might expect that a person a judge has found too ill for trial would leave jail for a hospital within days. In Alabama restoration has mostly meant a bed at Taylor Hardin Secure Medical Facility in Tuscaloosa, the state's forensic hospital, and there have not been enough beds or enough staff to run them. (The Department's own primer names Taylor Hardin for men and Bryce Hospital for women
.) So people wait where they already are, which is the county jail. In 2025 the average wait was more than a year, and more than thirty people had waited over two
A federal court is already supervising the problem. A class action now captioned
was settled in 2018 with a consent decree, an agreement between the two sides that a judge has made binding
. As the Associated Press describes its terms, the state has 60 days to complete an evaluation and 30 more to admit the person for restoration
monitors compliance. In March 2025 the part of the decree covering inpatient restoration was extended to 31 January 2027
The list of people waiting stood at 327 in January 2026 and 291 in July, against a Department goal of 100 by the end of the year

. Taylor Hardin has grown from 140 beds to 225, about 200 of which were filled in August 2026. A telehealth program restored 32 people inside county jails between the summer of 2025 and August 2026. Staff called
go through the list looking for people who might be better served outside the forensic system
. Beds are only useful with people to staff them, though, and in August 2024
told her board that about half of Taylor Hardin's technician and nursing positions were filled
Alabama has been here before. In

, decided in 1971, a federal court held that people confined in the state's psychiatric institutions had a constitutional right to adequate treatment, and the Department stayed under court supervision until 2003
The other live case is about a different group altogether.

concerns people serving sentences in state prisons, which are run by the Department of Corrections. In 2017 a federal judge found the prisons' mental health care "horrendously inadequate" and in violation of the

. On 24 June 2026 the appeals court upheld that finding and the system-wide injunction. It reversed a specific staffing mandate and some requirements for suicide-resistant cells, and sent those questions back to the trial court
Section 10 has the fullest account, under

. Domain 3 gives the hospital figures, and Domain 4 explains why staffing at Taylor Hardin decides how long people sit in jail. Domain 1 makes the wider point that court orders are still doing work that policy has not done
As you read, keep the measures apart. The waitlist is a count of people on a given day
, while the decree's deadlines are measured in days per person
. Taylor Hardin's bed count is capacity, and capacity matters only when the beds are staffed and open
. January 2027 is the date to watch.

title: The continuum of care
one_liner: Mental health services laid out as a line from prevention to recovery, and why the rungs between a hospital bed and an ordinary life matter as much as the bed.
why_here: Domain 3 is organized along the continuum, and every other domain has a 'Continuum lens' passage that asks where along it Alabama is strong or thin. The report's recurring phrase 'the middle of the continuum' only makes sense with the picture in mind.

further_reading.title: Pinals and Fuller, Beyond Beds: The Vital Role of a Full Continuum of Psychiatric Care (2017)
National Academies, Preventing Mental, Emotional, and Behavioral Disorders Among Young People, chapter 3: Defining the Scope of Prevention

self_check.q: A state doubles its psychiatric hospital beds but adds no step-down housing and no follow-up after discharge. What does the continuum idea predict?
options: Waiting lists disappear, because beds were the only shortage.
Demand for outpatient care falls, because more people are treated in hospital.
The new beds fill and stay full, because people ready to leave have nowhere to go, or leave unsupported and return.
Crisis calls stop, because hospitals take over crisis work.
self_check.explanation: A bed frees up only when the person in it can move to the next level. Capacity at one level depends on the levels beside it.

self_check.q: When this report says Alabama needs to 'fill the middle of the continuum', which services does it mean?
options: The rungs between a hospital or crisis bed and independent life, such as step-down residential care and supported housing.
The six crisis centers, because crisis response is the third of the five stops along the line.
Services for middle-income families, who earn too much for Medicaid and too little for private care.
The community mental health centers that serve the central counties of the state.
self_check.explanation: 'The middle' is the report's shorthand for the rungs a person steps down through after acute care. It is not the centre box of the diagram.

self_check.q: In the 2025 reporting year 259 people were in supported housing, out of 94,410 people served by the public system. What can you conclude from those two numbers alone?
options: Only 259 of the people served by the public system needed help with housing that year.
The other 94,151 people served were homeless or in shelters at the time.
Supported housing received no state or federal funding in that reporting year.
The service reaches a very small share of people served; the numbers do not say how many needed it.
self_check.explanation: The figures show reach, not need. Nobody has published a count of how many people would qualify for supported housing or are waiting for it.

body: When a state's mental health system makes the news, the story is usually about beds. There are too few of them, people wait in emergency rooms and jails, and replacing what was lost would cost a fortune.
of care is a correction to that picture, and it comes from an unexpected quarter. In 2017 the national association of state mental health directors published a paper called
, the same group whose minimum of 30 beds per 100,000 residents Alabama uses as its planning benchmark
. The paper's argument fits in a sentence: "24/7 inpatient care represents only a single component of a well-functioning

A continuum is a line of services ordered by intensity. The National Academies' version begins before anyone is ill, with promotion aimed at everybody and prevention aimed at people at risk. It then runs through treatment to what it calls maintenance, meaning long-term care and rehabilitation
. This report marks five stops along the line:
Two tests come with the picture, and the report borrows both. Does each level exist at enough scale? And do the hand-offs between levels work

? The second test is easy to forget. Nobody stays at one level. A person stabilized in hospital needs a clinic appointment the following week, perhaps a supervised place to live for some months, and in time a job. Take away the next rung and that person either stays put, in a bed someone else is waiting for, or leaves without support and comes back.
The key idea in one picture
Draw five boxes in a row, left to right: "promotion and prevention", "outpatient treatment", "crisis response", "inpatient and forensic care", "recovery supports"
. Join each neighbouring pair with a two-headed arrow labelled "hand-off". Between "inpatient and forensic care" and "recovery supports", add a sixth box with a dashed outline, labelled "

", and mark it "the middle". Under the crisis and inpatient boxes write "built up since 2020". Under the dashed box write "no statewide count of beds published". Under "recovery supports" write "259 in supported housing, 234 in
Alabama has spent the years since 2020 building the two parts of the line that deal with emergencies. The
, which hardly existed before, now has
. On the inpatient side the Department counted 771
in January 2026 and would like about twice that, to reach the 30-per-100,000 benchmark
. Those are the numbers legislators argue over.
The everyday level is outpatient care. It runs through the 19
, which are the way in for therapy, medication,
. Further along, the line gets thin. In the 2025
259 people were in supported housing and 234 in supported employment, out of 94,410 people the public system served.
, in which a team looks after people who would otherwise be in and out of hospital, reached 897

This is what the report means when it says the middle is missing. "The middle" is not the centre of the diagram. It is everything that lies between a locked ward and a life of one's own: step-down residential care, intensive outpatient programs, supported housing. The Department does pay for a ladder of residential services through its contracts with the centers, but no statewide count of those beds was found in its published reports as of October 2026
. So Alabama publishes its hospital beds to the last one and gives no figure at all for the places people go when they leave.
Money explains some of the pattern. In the report's reading, state dollars concentrate on crisis and inpatient care, while outpatient treatment and recovery supports depend on
, and so on whether a person has coverage

. A word of warning about vocabulary, too. Written with capitals, a "Continuum of Care" is a regional homelessness planning body recognized by the federal housing department, and Alabama has nine of them
. Section 11 uses the phrase in that sense only.

Domain 3 is the continuum set out service by service, so begin there. Then look for the short "Continuum lens" passage in each of the other domains, which puts the same question to money, staff, buildings and data in turn. Section 11 takes up housing and employment as systems in their own right. Section 12 explains why the new
payment, which pays one clinic for crisis care, outpatient treatment and follow-up together, is the report's main hope for mending the hand-offs

When you read a proposal for more beds or another crisis center, ask what the report asks. Where does the person go next, and who is paid to see that they get there? title: The crisis system
one_liner: Someone to contact, someone to respond, a safe place for help: the three parts of a crisis system, and how far each one reaches in Alabama.
why_here: Domain 3 describes Alabama's crisis services under these three headings, Domains 2 and 6 follow their money and their data, and Section 10 treats them as the first chance to keep a person out of jail.

further_reading.title: SAMHSA, 2025 National Guidelines for a Behavioral Health Coordinated System of Crisis Care
Alabama Department of Mental Health, Alabama Crisis System of Care
Alabama Department of Mental Health, 988 in Alabama

self_check.q: Alabama's in-state answer rate for 988 rose to 87.4 percent in FY2025. What does that figure tell you?
options: The share of calls answered by a counselor in Alabama and not passed to a national backup. It is silent on what happened next.
The share of callers whose crisis was resolved on the phone, without a mobile team or a visit to a center.
The share of Alabama's 67 counties whose residents can reach one of the four call centers.
The share of calls that were answered within the average answering time the Department reports.
self_check.explanation: It is a measure of who answered, not of outcome. A high rate means the caller probably reached someone who knows local services.

self_check.q: A rural county's residents can reach 988, but the county has no mobile crisis team and the nearest crisis center is two hours away. Under the three-part model, what happens when a caller needs help in person?
options: Nothing changes, because 988 is the whole of the crisis system.
The call is transferred to the national backup center, which sends a team.
Medicaid arranges a hospital admission.
The counselor can talk and refer, but the in-person response falls back on police and the emergency room.
self_check.explanation: The parts depend on each other. Without someone to respond and somewhere to go, a call line has only the old options to offer.

self_check.q: The state evaluator put crisis-center utilization at 27 percent in FY2024. The Department says most centers are at capacity most days. What is the most reasonable reading?
options: The centers were closed to walk-ins and drop-offs for most of the year.
Only 27 percent of the people who came to a center were admitted to a bed.
The two sides count capacity and use differently, so the figure means little without its definition.
One of the two must have falsified its figures, and the Legislature has to decide which.
self_check.explanation: The Department's printed response questions how utilization was calculated. The dispute is about method, which is why the report asks for shared definitions.

body: For most of living memory, a mental health emergency in America has been handled by whoever answers 911. Police arrive. The person ends up in an emergency room or a cell, and neither was built for them. Federal guidance issued in 2025 describes what should exist in place of that, and reduces it to three things:
, someone to respond, and a safe place for help
The first is a phone line. Since July 2022 that has meant
, the national three-digit number for mental health, substance use and suicide crises
, which in the guidance's words delivers "rapid, on-site interventions to de-escalate crises and connect individuals to care"
. The third is a place that is neither a hospital ward nor a jail, a
where a person can walk in or be brought and be seen straight away.
The guidance wants the three to work as one system serving "anyone, anywhere, at anytime"
. The reasoning is practical. A call line with no team to send and nowhere to refer can only talk. A crisis center that officers have never heard of stays quiet. Each part is worth far less alone.
The key idea in one picture
Draw three boxes in a row. The first is "Someone to contact: 988, four in-state call centers"
. The second is "Someone to respond: mobile crisis teams, 14 teams at 11 centers"
. The third is "A safe place for help: six crisis centers and one pediatric unit"

. Two arrows leave the 988 box, one to each of the others, both labelled "triage". Two arrows enter the crisis-center box from outside the row: "walk-in" and "law-enforcement drop-off, around the clock". A loop on the mobile-team box is labelled "follow-up for up to 72 hours". Below the row, draw two boxes with dashed outlines, "emergency room" and "jail", and label them "what crisis care is meant to relieve".
Alabama built its crisis system almost from nothing after 2020, and it now has all three elements
. That is a real achievement. The harder questions are how far each element reaches and whether anyone can show what it accomplishes.
Start with the phone. Four call centers inside the state answer 988, and in

title: The eight domains
one_liner: Why this report describes Alabama's mental health system by the jobs a system has to do, and where the list of jobs comes from.
why_here: Part II is organized as Domain 1 to Domain 8 and Part III as Section 9 to Section 12. Knowing what each one asks, and why crisis centers or beds turn up in several of them, makes the whole report easier to use.

further_reading.title: WHO, Everybody's Business: Strengthening Health Systems to Improve Health Outcomes (2007 framework for action)
WHO, Monitoring the Building Blocks of Health Systems (2010), cover and contents
Alabama Department of Mental Health, Strategic Plan: Priorities & Goals

self_check.q: The report discusses the six crisis centers in Domain 2, Domain 3, Domain 5, Domain 6 and Section 10. What does that tell you about how the report is built?
options: The crisis centers are run by five different agencies, and each agency is described in its own domain.
Each domain asks a different question of the same service: its cost, its work, its buildings, its data, its link to the courts.
The report repeats itself, so a reader can take the first mention and skip the other four.
Crisis centers are the only Alabama service that fits every one of WHO's building blocks.
self_check.explanation: The domains are functions, so one program shows up wherever its money, staff, buildings or data are being discussed. The repetition is the design.

self_check.q: WHO's six building blocks describe what a health system does. Why would a report built on them need to add domains on equity and on community engagement?
options: Because WHO requires member states to add two blocks of their own.
Because Alabama law names equity and engagement as duties of the Department of Mental Health.
Because a list of functions can be fully staffed and funded and still not show who is being missed or how the public influences the system.
Because the six blocks apply only to physical health.
self_check.explanation: The six blocks check whether the jobs are being done. Who benefits, and who has a say, are separate questions, and neither is among WHO's six.

self_check.q: At the end of Domain 4 you read 'ADMH plan goals touched: C1, C2, C3'. You want to quote this to a legislator. What is the accurate way to describe those codes?
options: They are goal numbers printed in the Department's public strategic plan, under each of its five priorities.
They are federal reporting codes that every state uses in its block-grant application.
They are section numbers in the chapter of the Code of Alabama that sets up the Department.
They are Little Orange Fish's own numbering; the Department's public page shows five priorities and no goal numbers.
self_check.explanation: The codes come from the publisher's alignment analysis of the full plan. Cite the Department for the five priorities and the report for the goal codes.

body: Ask most people to describe a state's mental health system and they will start drawing an organization chart, with the department at the top and its hospitals and offices underneath. The World Health Organization starts somewhere else. Its 2007 framework set out "to promote a common understanding of what a health system is", and the answer it gave was a list of jobs that any health system has to do, whoever happens to do them
There are six. WHO calls them building blocks: service delivery, the health workforce, health information systems, access to essential medicines, financing, and leadership and governance

. The scheme does not say which agency owns which job, and that is why it is useful. A state can be checked block by block. Is anyone governing? Is the money there, and whose money is it? Are there enough trained people to do the work? The blocks also lean on each other, so a clinic can be fully funded and still sit half empty for want of staff.
This report takes the six and adds two of its own. Equity asks who the system reaches and who it misses. Community engagement asks how the public shapes it. Neither is among WHO's six

. Together they make the eight domains of Part II. Four more sections follow in Part III, on children and families, the justice system, housing and social conditions, and payers, because a good deal of what decides a person's care in Alabama happens outside the
The key idea in one picture
Draw two rows of boxes. The top row has six boxes, one for each WHO building block

. The bottom row has eight, labelled Domain 1 to Domain 8. Six arrows run downward: leadership and governance to Domain 1 (governance, policy and law); financing to Domain 2; service delivery to Domain 3; health workforce to Domain 4; access to essential medicines to Domain 5, which the report widens to technology and infrastructure; health information systems to Domain 6. Domain 7 (equity) and Domain 8 (community engagement) receive no arrow and carry the label "added by this report". To the right, a separate column of four boxes holds Section 9 (children, youth and families), Section 10 (justice), Section 11 (housing and
) and Section 12 (payers), under the heading "systems beyond the Department".
A map of functions suits Alabama because responsibility here is scattered. The Department of Mental Health is the
sets the covered services and rates that determine what providers can bill
and, in its 2026 session, attached conditions to them
. An organization chart of the Department would leave all of that off the page.
Follow one thing through the report and the design shows itself. The six
appear in Domain 3 as a service, a place that takes walk-ins and police drop-offs around the clock
. In Domain 2 they are a $36 million line in the

. Domain 5 treats them as buildings, with capital costs the state evaluator put at between $3.3 million and $12.6 million a center. Domain 6 treats them as a measurement problem, since the same evaluator could not verify the centers'
. Section 10 meets them once more, as the earliest point at which someone can be steered away from jail. Five appearances, five different questions. The repetition is deliberate.
Each domain is also held up against two yardsticks. One is
of care: a short "Continuum lens" passage asks where, along the line from prevention to recovery, the domain is strong or thin
. The other is the state's own plan. The Department's Strategic Plan 2025–2028 has five priorities
, and each domain closes with a line listing the plan goals it touches. Treat those codes, A1 to E3, with some care. They are
's numbering, taken from its own analysis of the full plan document, and the Department's public page shows only the five priority headings

Use the domains as an index of questions. If you want to know who decides something, start in Domain 1. If you want to know why something already decided has not happened, the answer is usually in Domain 2 or Domain 4. Domain 4 says of itself that every other domain depends on it, and the
shows why: in August 2024 only about half of its technician and nursing positions were filled
The four sections of Part III each borrow a frame of their own, and each frame has a primer on this site. Section 9 reads children's services against the

. Section 12, on payers, is where the coverage questions raised in several domains are worked out in full. One caution applies throughout: the "Gaps and opportunities" bullets that close each domain are the report's own reading of the evidence, and should be quoted as analysis and not as the finding of any agency.

title: How Alabama funds mental health
one_liner: The streams of money behind the Department of Mental Health, which of them the Legislature votes on each year, and how conditions get attached.
why_here: Domain 2 is built on these funding streams, and Domains 1, 3 and 6 keep returning to the conditions the Legislature placed on crisis money in the FY2027 budget. You need the difference between the General Fund, earmarked funds, federal money and one-time settlement money to follow any of it.

Alabama Department of Mental Health, Annual Report FY25 (financial tables)
Code of Alabama §28-3-202 (liquor tax and the Alabama Special Mental Health Fund)
SAMHSA, Community Mental Health Services Block Grant

self_check.q: The General Fund supplied about one-sixth of the Department of Mental Health's revenue in FY2025. Why does the report still treat that line as the one to watch?
options: Because it is the largest single source of the Department's money, ahead of Medicaid and federal grants.
Because it pays for what Medicaid does not, such as crisis centers, and is decided afresh each year.
Because federal law requires the General Fund to match the block grant dollar for dollar each year.
Because it is the only source that may be spent on developmental-disability services in the community.
self_check.explanation: Medicaid is the largest source, but it follows enrolled people and covered services. The General Fund is the flexible money, and the Legislature sets it every session.

self_check.q: The FY2027 General Fund line for 988 call centers is zero, while opioid-settlement appropriations in 2025 and 2026 each included money for 988. What is the risk in that arrangement?
options: Settlement money cannot legally be spent on a crisis line, so the appropriation may be struck down.
Settlement money is counted twice in the Department's revenue, which inflates its reported budget.
The federal government will reduce Alabama's Medicaid match by the amount of settlement money spent.
Settlement appropriations are one-time, so the service has no standing claim on next year's budget.
self_check.explanation: An ongoing service is being carried by money that has to be appropriated again each time. Nothing it pays for recurs automatically.

self_check.q: As reported, the FY2027 budget withholds the last two quarterly installments of the crisis money until the Department reports on the programs. What kind of action is that?
options: A condition on an appropriation: the money is appropriated, and its release depends on the agency reporting.
A cut: the crisis programs lose half of their funding for the year, whatever the Department does.
A federal penalty, imposed through the block grant after the evaluation commission's report.
A transfer of the crisis centers from the Department of Mental Health to the Legislature's own staff.
self_check.explanation: The amount is unchanged. The Legislature is using the timing of payment as leverage to obtain information.

body: Every spring the Alabama Legislature debates how much to give the
, and a number is reported in the press. For
. It is easy to take that for the state's mental health budget. It is about one-sixth of what the Department actually takes in.
The state passes two main budgets each year, one for the
, and an agency can spend only what those acts appropriate to it
. The fiscal year runs from 1 October to 30 September, so "FY2027" begins in October 2026
lasts one year. A program funded this session has no claim on the next.
Not all money comes that way, though. Some arrives by standing law: a tax is earmarked for a purpose and flows to it without an annual vote. Some is federal, either as the match on
is a federal sum a state receives each year to spend on community mental health services, with a few obligations attached
. And some is one-time money, of which the
The key idea in one picture
Draw one horizontal bar labelled "Department of Mental Health operating revenue, FY2025: $1.43 billion"
. Divide it into five segments, left to right: "General Fund, 16.8%", "

, 16.5%", "Education Trust Fund, 5.5%", "other state sources", and a long final segment, "federal, local and miscellaneous, 59.1%, mostly Medicaid". Above the bar, draw an arrow into the General Fund segment from a box reading "Legislature, yearly General Fund act", and hang a tag on that arrow: "conditions can be attached"
. A second arrow runs into the Education Trust Fund segment from "Legislature, yearly education budget". An arrow into the Special Mental Health Fund segment comes from "taxes earmarked by statute"
. Below the bar, an arrow into the last segment comes from "
on Medicaid claims, plus grants". Off to one side, a box with a dashed outline reads "opioid-settlement appropriations: one-time".

The Department's operating revenue in FY2025 was $1.43 billion. State sources supplied 40.9 percent of it. The General Fund gave $239.8 million, or 16.8 percent, and the Special Mental Health Fund almost exactly as much, $236.4 million. The Education Trust Fund added $79.1 million. Everything else, 59.1 percent, was federal, local and miscellaneous money, and most of that was Medicaid
Two things in those figures surprise people. The first is how much of the Department's budget is not about mental illness at all. Medicaid paid $568.0 million for community
services, against $125.9 million for community mental-illness services
. The second is the Special Mental Health Fund, which rarely makes the news. State law sends part of a liquor tax into it and says the fund "shall be used only for mental health purposes"

So why the attention to the General Fund? Because it is the money with choices in it. Medicaid follows the people who are enrolled and the services it covers. In the report's reading, the General Fund pays for what Medicaid does not:
care for the uninsured, and services for adults without coverage
. In December 2024 the Department was considering a request for a General Fund increase of $68.6 million for FY2026
. The enacted increase was about $4.7 million, and the FY2027 figure is lower again
The 2026 session added something new. A state
had reported the previous September that it could not verify the crisis centers' results
. As reported on final passage, the FY2027 budget withholds the last two
centers until the Department reports the status of the programs to the budget chairs, the Finance Director and the
. An earlier Senate committee version had spelled out what to report: each center's operating expenses, employees and persons served
. The comparison sheets most people consult show amounts only. The condition sits in the text of the act, which could not be read for this report.
Settlement money has become a second channel. Act 2025-255 directed $27.9 million of opioid-settlement funds to the Department, including $3.5 million for
, appropriated a further $43.1 million across agencies, of which $26.4 million went to the Department
. Meanwhile the General Fund line for 988 call centers went from $500,000 in FY2026 to zero in FY2027
. The weakness is that nothing settlement funds pay for recurs without a base appropriation.
Federal block grants are small by comparison, at $33.8 million in FY2025
, but they carry weight. Accepting the grant obliges the state to keep a
that includes people who use services
on which most national comparisons of Alabama rest

Domain 2 lays out the revenue, the budget lines for FY2026 and FY2027, and the spending benchmarks. Read its table of General Fund lines beside the paragraph on settlement funds, and ask of each service which of the two is paying for it
. Domain 1 treats the FY2027 conditions as a change in how the Department is governed, and Domain 6 argues that agreed measures, published in advance, would let such conditions be met with data
You will also meet two cost estimates for psychiatric beds, $226.4 million from the Department and about $590 million from the House budget chair
. The sources do not reconcile them, and neither is an appropriation.

title: Medicaid and the coverage gap
one_liner: Who Medicaid covers in a state that has not expanded it, how the federal match works, and the two ways a state changes its program.
why_here: Domain 2 and Section 12 turn on who pays for care, and Domain 7 treats coverage as the main equity question. Almost every section refers to the coverage gap, a state plan amendment or a Section 1115 waiver without stopping to explain them.

further_reading.title: KFF, How Many Uninsured Are in the Coverage Gap and How Many Could be Eligible if All States Adopted the Medicaid Expansion? (July 2026)
MACPAC, Matching rates
Medicaid.gov, About Section 1115 Demonstrations
Medicaid.gov, Medicaid State Plan Amendments

self_check.q: An Alabama adult with no children and no disability earns about half the federal poverty level. What help with health coverage is open to her?
options: Medicaid, because her income is well below the poverty line.
A subsidized marketplace plan, because subsidies are largest for the lowest incomes.
Neither. Alabama Medicaid does not cover adults like her at any income, and marketplace subsidies begin at the poverty line.
Medicare, because Alabama uses it to cover adults who do not qualify for Medicaid.
self_check.explanation: She is in the coverage gap: too much income for Alabama's Medicaid rules, which for her group means any income at all, and too little for marketplace subsidies.

self_check.q: KFF estimates 86,000 uninsured Alabama adults in the coverage gap and 147,000 who would become eligible if the state expanded Medicaid. Why is the second number larger?
options: Expansion reaches 138 percent of the poverty level, so it also takes in uninsured adults just above the poverty line.
The second number counts children in the gap as well as adults, and children outnumber adults in Medicaid.
The second number adds people who already have employer coverage but would switch to Medicaid.
The first number comes from 2024 survey data and the second is a projection for the year 2032.
self_check.explanation: The gap ends at the poverty line, where marketplace subsidies start. Expansion would go higher, so the eligible group is bigger than the gap.

self_check.q: Alabama added mobile crisis services by state plan amendment and inpatient psychiatric stays in two counties by Section 1115 waiver. Why does the difference matter to someone planning services?
options: A state plan amendment needs no federal approval, while a waiver does.
A waiver is paid entirely with state money, while an amendment draws the federal match.
An amendment applies only to children, while a waiver applies only to adults.
An amendment is a standing change to the program, while a waiver is a time-limited experiment that has to be renewed.
self_check.explanation: Both need federal approval and both draw the match. The waiver has an end date, May 2027 in Alabama's case, and its future has to be decided before then.

body: is usually described as health insurance for the poor, and in most of the country that is close enough. Each state runs its own program inside federal rules, and Washington pays a share of every dollar spent. The share is called the
, or FMAP. It comes from a formula that gives "higher reimbursement to states with lower per capita incomes", with a floor of 50 percent and a ceiling of 83
. Alabama's rate sits well up that range, at 72.63 percent for
. So for each dollar of Medicaid care, the state has to find about 27 cents.
Who may enrol is the part a state controls, and this is where expectations go wrong. The Affordable Care Act let states open Medicaid to all adults with incomes up to 138 percent of the
. Forty-one states, counting the District of Columbia, have done so. Alabama is one of the ten that have not

The same law built the insurance marketplaces on the assumption that every state would expand. Premium subsidies were set to begin at the poverty line, because anyone poorer was supposed to have Medicaid. Then expansion became optional, and in KFF's words "poor adults living in states that decided not to expand were left without an affordable coverage option"
. An adult just above the poverty line can buy subsidized insurance. One just below it cannot.
The key idea in one picture

Draw two vertical bars side by side, each a scale of income from 0 at the bottom to 150 percent of the federal poverty level at the top. The left bar is labelled "Alabama parent". Shade the band from 0 to about 18 percent and label it "Medicaid"
. Shade the band from about 18 to 100 percent in a contrasting colour and label it "coverage gap: no Medicaid, no
subsidy". Label everything from 100 percent upward "marketplace subsidies"
. The right bar is labelled "Alabama adult without children or a disability". Here the gap band runs from 0 to 100 percent, with marketplace subsidies above it
. Across both bars draw a dashed horizontal line at 138 percent, labelled "Medicaid limit in the 41
A parent in Alabama qualifies only with income up to about 18 percent of the poverty level
, and an adult with no dependent children and no disability does not qualify at any income
How many people are in the gap depends on who is counting.
, which campaigns for expansion, puts it at up to 155,000
. KFF's estimate from 2024 survey data is 86,000 uninsured adults in the gap itself and 147,000 who would become eligible if the state expanded
. The larger KFF number reaches above the poverty line, to 138 percent, and so takes in people who can already buy subsidized marketplace plans. The two should not be averaged.
For mental health the consequence is direct. Medicaid is the largest single funder of the care the
. A service Medicaid pays for can grow. A person Medicaid does not cover has to be paid for from somewhere else, and that somewhere is mostly the state's
. Among Alabama adults with any mental illness, 14.1 percent are uninsured, against 9.2 percent nationally
When Alabama wants to change what its Medicaid program does, it has two instruments. A
alters the standing agreement between the state and the federal government
teams became a Medicaid benefit this way in October 2023

is permission to do something the ordinary rules forbid. Waivers are approved as experiments, generally for five years, and must not cost the federal government more than it would otherwise have spent
. Alabama holds one. Medicaid has historically not paid for adults aged 21 to 64 in a psychiatric institution of more than 16 beds
, and the waiver lifts that rule for facilities in Mobile and Baldwin counties until May 2027
. A second waiver, for substance use treatment, has been pending with the federal Medicaid agency since July 2023
Unlike most states, Alabama does not hand Medicaid to private health plans. It has no comprehensive
, which is why the state could introduce the
The terms of the expansion debate shifted in 2025. A federal budget law ended, from January 2026, the temporary extra match that had been offered to states expanding for the first time
that states use to raise their own share, and were Alabama to expand, its 6 percent hospital tax would have to fall to 3.5 percent by FY2032

Section 12 has the full account, and Domain 2 places Medicaid among the Department's revenues. Domain 7 reads it as an equity question, and Section 10 asks what happens to a person's Medicaid on the way into jail and out again. Domain 1 says of coverage policy that it affects more sections of the report than any other single decision

When you read about a new service, ask which payer it belongs to. If the answer is Medicaid, check whether it arrived by state plan amendment or by waiver, since a waiver comes with an end date. If the answer is the General Fund, you are probably looking at something Medicaid does not cover, or at care for people it does not reach

title: Reading the indicators
one_liner: How to read the report's rates, rankings and counts without asking them to say more than they can.
why_here: Domain 6 and the baseline tables are built from federal and state indicators, and every other section quotes them. The previous edition of this report misread two of them, which is a fair warning to the rest of us.

further_reading.title: SAMHSA, 2025 Uniform Reporting System Output Tables: Alabama
Mental Health America, The State of Mental Health in America 2025
HUD, 2025 Continuum of Care Homeless Populations and Subpopulations: Alabama
NRI, State Mental Health Agency Expenditures and Funding Sources, FY2001 to FY2024

self_check.q: Alabama's 30-day readmission rate to state hospitals went from 6.8 percent in 2024 to 1.5 percent in 2025. Which statement is the most defensible?
options: Discharge planning improved more than fourfold in a single year.
Alabama's state hospitals now perform six times better than the national average.
The rate moved because four fewer people were readmitted, out of about 70 discharges; that is too few to call a trend.
The 2024 figure must have been an error, since rates do not fall that fast.
self_check.explanation: Five of 74 became one of 68. With so few discharges, each person moves the rate by more than a percentage point.

self_check.q: Alabama's public system served 18.31 people per 1,000 residents in 2025, against 22.94 nationally. What does that support?
options: Mental illness is less common in Alabama than in the country as a whole, by about a fifth.
Alabama's public system reaches fewer people for its population than average; the figure cannot say why.
About 18 percent of Alabamians received mental health care from some source in 2025.
Fewer Alabamians use privately paid mental health care than people in other states.
self_check.explanation: The rate counts people served by the state mental health authority. Care paid for privately is outside it, and so is everyone who needed care and got none.

self_check.q: One sentence in the report says 2.7 percent of people served were homeless in 2025. Another says 4.1 percent. Both come from the same federal tables for the same year. What explains the difference?
options: The first figure covers everyone served, children included; the second covers adults only.
The first figure is for fiscal year 2025 and the second for calendar year 2025.
One of the two is a provisional estimate that was later revised.
The first counts rural counties and the second counts urban ones.
self_check.explanation: The all-ages row includes children and the adult row does not, so the two answer different questions. Check which one a sentence is using before you compare.

body: An indicator is a number that stands in for something you cannot see directly. Nobody can watch a mental health system "reach" people, so we count the people it served and divide by the population
. That fraction is the indicator. It is only as good as the choices packed inside it: who was counted on top, who was counted underneath, over which months, and by whom.

Those choices are easy to lose sight of, even for careful people. The 2025 edition of this report said that 17.4 percent of the people Alabama's public system served were Black. That was the national figure. Alabama's share was more than twice as high, and stood at 38.3 percent in 2025
. The same edition gave an employment rate of 45.5 percent, which was the share employed among clients in the labor force. Among all adult clients whose status was known it was 20.5 percent
. Neither number was invented. Each was a real figure answering a different question from the one the sentence asked.
Most of the comparisons in this report come from one place, the federal
tables. Every state files them as a condition of its
, and the federal agency publishes them beside national figures
. Others come from organizations that rank states, from one-night counts, and from the Department's own annual report. Each kind has its own habits.
The key idea in one picture
Draw a large fraction in the middle of the page. The top reads "1 person readmitted within 30 days". The bottom reads "68 civil discharges from
". To the right, an equals sign and "1.5%"
. Four labels with pointers surround it. Pointing at the bottom of the fraction: "Who is counted? Civil patients,
, state hospitals only." Pointing at the whole fraction: "When?

2025, which is October 2024 to September 2025." Pointing at the result: "Compared with what? United States, 9.0%." Pointing at the top: "How many events? One." Beneath, in smaller type, draw the same fraction for 2024, "5 of 74 = 6.8%"
, joined to the first by an arrow labelled "four fewer people".
Start with the measure the report uses most. The
is the number of people the public system served for every 1,000 residents. Alabama's was 18.31 in 2025, the same as the year before, against 22.94 for the country

. It is tempting to read that as unmet need. The number will not bear it. People treated through private insurance are not in it, and a low rate could reflect less need, poorer access or simply a smaller public role.
Small numbers are the next trap. Alabama's 30-day
to state hospitals fell from 6.8 percent to 1.5 percent in a year, far below the national 9.0. Behind those percentages are five readmissions among 74 discharges, then one among 68
. Four people account for the whole change.
Rankings need a different kind of care.
ranks 51 jurisdictions, and by its convention a rank near 51 is bad

. Alabama is 50th on its youth measures. Look underneath, though, and the picture is more specific. About as many Alabama young people have a major depressive episode as elsewhere, 18.9 percent. What is exceptional is that 66.4 percent of them got no treatment, the highest share in the country
. A rank tells you the order of the states and nothing about the distance between them, nor about which part of the measure is doing the work.
runs from October to September, and the federal reporting year covers the same months
. Deaths are counted by calendar year. The same program can therefore produce two honest totals: the opioid council's report gives 48,179 boxes of
distributed between November 2024 and October 2025, and 40,733 kits in fiscal year 2025
. Some figures are also provisional. The council's 2025 overdose count of 1,052 is an early estimate, and its 2024 figure of at least 1,151 is a floor, so the pair should not be read as a decline
One-night counts have their own limits. The homelessness figure comes from a count made by local coalitions on a single night: 4,601 people in 2024 and 4,137 in 2025
. The federal housing department itself cautions that "the reliability and consistency of the homeless counts may also vary" from one coalition to another
Last, watch the words. "Rural" means 55 of 67 counties in one sentence and 42 percent of residents in another, and those are different measurements
has been assigned to it, which is a statement about responsibility and not about the drive

Domain 6 has the main table of federal measures and the list of what Alabama does not publish. Appendix B carries the baseline indicators. Wherever the report gives an Alabama figure it tries to give the comparison, the period and the source key beside it, so use them
On the site's maps, apply the same habits. A shaded county tells you what the legend says and no more. If the legend says "assigned to a crisis center", it is not a map of access
. And when a number seems to settle an argument, look for its denominator first.

title: The Sequential Intercept Model
one_liner: Six points between a mental health crisis and a prison sentence at which a person can be steered toward care, and who holds each one in Alabama.
why_here: Section 10 is organized intercept by intercept, and Domains 1, 3 and 4 refer to the intercepts when they discuss police training, courts and the forensic waitlist. The model tells you which local official can act on which problem.

further_reading.title: SAMHSA, The Sequential Intercept Model (SIM)
SAMHSA GAINS Center, The Sequential Intercept Model: Advancing Community-Based Solutions (brochure)

self_check.q: A county opens a mental health court for defendants with serious mental illness. In the model's terms, what has the county added, and what has it left untouched?
options: It has added an Intercept 0 service, so fewer people in crisis will need to call 988.
It has added an option at Intercept 3, for people already charged; arrest and booking are untouched.
It has covered all six intercepts, because a court can order any service a defendant needs.
It has added an Intercept 5 program, because courts supervise people on parole and probation.
self_check.explanation: A treatment court works on people who are already in the court system. The earlier chances, at the crisis call, the police encounter and the booking desk, belong to other agencies.

self_check.q: Why does the model put community crisis services at Intercept 0, ahead of law enforcement?
options: Because crisis services are run by the police in most states.
Because Intercept 0 was added last and the numbering could not be changed.
Because a crisis line, a mobile team or a crisis center can settle a crisis before any officer is involved.
Because crisis services cost less than any other intercept.
self_check.explanation: The intercepts are in the order a person meets them. The earliest diversion is the one that happens before the justice system is in the picture at all.

self_check.q: Section 10's summary table shows, for Intercept 2, that no statewide jail-screening standard and no count of commitments or jail suicides were found. What is the right reading of that blank?
options: Alabama publishes nothing that would show whether people are being identified and diverted at that point.
Nothing happens at Intercept 2 in Alabama.
County jails in Alabama do not hold people with mental illness.
Intercept 2 is handled by the federal courts and so is outside the report.
self_check.explanation: Things certainly happen at booking and first appearance. The gap is in standards and published data, which is why the report suggests a statewide booking screen with counts.

body: " and most people picture a single moment, an officer deciding not to make an arrest. The

starts from the observation that there are several such moments, spread over months or years, and that each one is in different hands. Three researchers, Mark Munetz, Patricia Griffin and Henry Steadman, developed it in the early 2000s

. The federal center that promotes it calls it "a conceptual model to inform community-based responses to the involvement of people with mental and substance use disorders in the criminal justice system"

The model lays the justice system out as a path and marks six places along it. They are numbered from 0 to 5: community services, law enforcement, initial detention and first court hearings, jails and courts,
. At each place there is something that can be done. A

can go out where a patrol car would have gone. A brief screen at the booking desk, which the federal brochure says can be given to everyone by staff with no clinical training, can flag a person before the first hearing. A treatment court can supervise someone through care. A jail can plan a person's release so that medication does not stop at the gate

Two things follow from drawing it this way. Earlier is better, because every intercept a person passes means more time in custody. And no single agency owns the path. Communities use the model, in its own words, to "identify gaps, resources, and opportunities at each intercept"
. It is a map for finding out who should be in the room.
The key idea in one picture

The justice system is a regular point of contact for Alabamians with mental illness. The director of the state's Crisis Intervention Team program estimates that 20 to 30 percent of the calls law enforcement fields involve a person in a mental health crisis

. Walk the six intercepts and a pattern appears. The state has built a good deal at the start of the path and is under court order further along it, and in between there is a stretch where very little is counted.

Intercept 2, the booking desk and the first court appearance, is the thinnest. No statewide standard for mental health screening at booking was found, and no statewide count of jail suicides. What exists is local. Morgan County's jail, to take the report's example, employs two licensed counselors

title: System of Care and the social determinants of health
one_liner: Two frameworks that look past the clinic: one for how children's services should fit together, one for the living conditions that shape mental health.
why_here: Section 9 reads Alabama's services for children against the System of Care principles, and Section 11 is organized by the five Healthy People 2030 domains. Both sections use the frameworks as checklists, so it helps to know what is on them.

further_reading.title: Stroul, Blau and Friedman, Updating the System of Care Concept and Philosophy (2010)
Stroul, Blau and Larson, The Evolution of the System of Care Approach (2021)
Healthy People 2030, Social Determinants of Health
Alabama Department of Mental Health, Child & Family Services

self_check.q: A 15-year-old with depression sees a school counselor, is covered by Medicaid and has a juvenile probation officer. What does the System of Care framework ask of the agencies involved?
options: That each agency treat the part of the problem that falls under its own budget and report separately.
That the juvenile court take charge, because it has legal authority over the others.
That the family choose one agency and drop the rest.
That the services be organized as one coordinated network around the young person and the family.
self_check.explanation: The framework's central claim is that children are served by several systems at once, so the systems have to plan together, with the family as a partner.

self_check.q: Alabama law already provides a Children's Policy Council and a State Team for children with multiple needs. Why does Section 9 still list cross-agency coordination as a gap?
options: Because both bodies were abolished by the Legislature in its 2025 session.
Because both have wider remits; none dedicated to children's mental health was identified.
Because the Department of Mental Health is not a member of either of the two bodies.
Because federal law forbids state agencies to share plans for individual children.
self_check.explanation: The two statutory bodies cover children's policy in general and children with multiple needs. The report found none whose business is children's mental health as such.

self_check.q: A clinic provides good treatment, but many of its patients lose their housing and stop coming. How would the social-determinants framework describe the problem?
options: As a sign that living conditions shape outcomes, so the housing system is part of the mental health picture.
As a failure of clinical quality, since good treatment should be enough to prevent homelessness.
As a matter outside mental health policy, to be left to housing agencies and local coalitions.
As evidence that the patients were misdiagnosed and needed a different kind of treatment.
self_check.explanation: Housing sits in the 'neighborhood and built environment' domain. The framework treats it as a cause of health outcomes, which is why Section 11 is in this report at all.

body: It is natural to think of mental health care as what happens in a clinic or a hospital. The two frameworks in this primer were both written to push against that habit. One concerns children
The System of Care idea dates from the mid-1980s, when a federal program for children's mental health services began and the concept was first set down

. Its premise is that a child with serious emotional difficulties is seldom the business of one agency alone. So the framework asks for services "organized into a coordinated network", one that "builds meaningful partnerships with families and youth"
. Three values sit at the core. Care should be driven by the family and guided by the young person. It should be based in the community. And it should fit the family's culture and language

Under those values come working principles: a broad array of services, a plan made for the individual child, links across the agencies that serve children, early identification, and help with the move into adulthood
. An update in 2021 kept all of these and added several more, among them
and the integration of mental health with physical health
, the federal government's set of national health goals, defines
of health as "the conditions in the environments where people are born, live, learn, work, play, worship, and age"
. It sorts them into five domains: economic stability, education access and quality, health care access and quality, neighborhood and built environment, and social and community context
. Income, housing and schooling shape a person's health alongside anything a doctor does.
The key idea in one picture
Draw two panels. In the left panel, put a circle labelled "child and family" at the centre. Around it place six boxes, each joined to the centre by a line: "

", "child welfare", "juvenile justice", "early-childhood education". Place a seventh box, "pediatric medicine", just outside the ring. Join the six boxes to one another with a dashed ring labelled "coordination across agencies: the principle. No standing body dedicated to children's mental health identified in Alabama". In the right panel, put a circle labelled "person" at the centre and five boxes around it, one for each Healthy People 2030 domain
. Under each domain name write the Alabama systems Section 11 files there: "economic stability: disability income,
, food assistance"; "education access and quality: school mental health services"; "health care access and quality: coverage,
, transport"; "neighborhood and built environment: housing, homelessness, broadband"; "social and community context: faith communities, veterans' network".

Section 9 counts at least six public systems that deliver children's mental health care in Alabama: the Department of Mental Health, the schools, Medicaid, child welfare, juvenile justice and early-childhood education, with pediatric medicine alongside. That is exactly the situation the System of Care was designed for. The Department took a step toward it in October 2023, when it gathered its own children's programs into a single
Office of Child and Family Services
Hold Alabama against the principles and the results are mixed. On the array of services, the Department's providers offer crisis,
, with at least one of these in every county
. On coordination the report found less. State law provides a
and a State Team for children with multiple needs, and both have remits wider than mental health
. No standing body dedicated to children's mental health was identified.
"Family-driven" has taken a particular form here. Since 2022 a school must have a parent's written
before providing mental health services, at first for students under 14, and since October 2025 for students under 16
. Whether that has changed how many students are served is not known, because no before-and-after count was found. The state has also been without a youth survey since 2021
A caution about the phrase. The Department's first strategic priority is also called "System of Care Transformation", and there it means the Department's service system as a whole
For the social determinants, Section 11 goes through the five domains in turn, and housing is where the mental health system's own gap shows most clearly. Alabama's 2025
found 4,137 people homeless, 502 of whom were recorded as
. In the same year 259 people were in

. Local homelessness planning belongs to nine regional coalitions called
, which are funded through the federal housing department and sit outside the mental health system altogether
. No state supportive-housing subsidy program was found as of October 2026.
Section 9 has a table that sets each System of Care principle beside what Alabama has. Notice which rows end with something not identified or not published
. Section 11 has a matching table for the five domains, giving the Alabama system, a published measure and a gap for each
The two sections also explain choices made elsewhere in the report. Schools appear in Domain 3 as part of prevention and again in Section 9 as the largest point of contact with children
