title: Measuring the workforce shortage
one_liner: Shortage-area designations, percent of need met, provider ratios, vacancies and licensure compacts: what each number does and does not tell you.
why_here: Domain 4 opens with four different measures of Alabama's workforce shortage, and Domains 3, 7 and Section 9 quote them again. They answer different questions, and one of them can look ordinary while another looks dire.

further_reading.title: HRSA Bureau of Health Workforce, What Is Shortage Designation?
KFF State Health Facts, Mental Health Care Health Professional Shortage Areas (HPSAs)
National Health Service Corps, NHSC Loan Repayment Program
Mental Health America, The State of Mental Health in America 2025

self_check.q: Alabama meets 28.4 percent of need in its mental health shortage areas, about the same as the country as a whole. Mental Health America ranks Alabama last for workforce availability. How can both be true?
options: One of the two sources must be out of date, since both draw on the same federal data.
The first counts psychiatrists inside shortage areas; the second counts every kind of provider across the whole state.
The first figure is for adults and the second is for children and adolescents under 18.
The ranking counts only providers who accept Medicaid, and Alabama has few of those.
self_check.explanation: They are different measures. A state can have a typical supply of psychiatrists in its shortage areas and still have far fewer counselors, social workers and psychologists per resident than other states.

self_check.q: Alabama is a member of the Counseling Compact. As of October 2026, can a counselor licensed in another member state use the compact to see clients in Alabama?
options: Yes, because membership takes effect on the day a state joins.
Yes, but only by telehealth and only in rural counties.
No, because Alabama withdrew from the compact in 2026.
Not yet. Ten states were issuing privileges by then and Alabama was not among them.
self_check.explanation: Joining a compact and operating it are separate steps. A compact adds no clinicians until privileges are being issued.

self_check.q: A legislator wants to know whether the provider rate increases funded for FY2024 helped community providers keep their staff. Which measure would answer that?
options: An updated count of vacancies and turnover in the provider network, which the Department has not published since the end of FY2023.
The number of federally designated shortage areas, which falls when providers keep staff.
Mental Health America's ranking, which is recalculated after each state budget.
The percent of need met, because it counts every clinician in the public system.
self_check.explanation: Designations, need met and the provider ratio describe supply across the state. Only the provider network's own staffing figures show what the money did, and the latest is from 2023.

body: It would be convenient if a shortage of mental health workers were a single number. It is at least four, collected by different bodies for different purposes, and they do not always agree. Two of them put Alabama in very different places
The first is the Health Professional Shortage Area, or
. The federal health workforce agency designates these, and a designation "can be geographic areas, populations, or facilities"

. One designation may cover a whole county and another a single prison or clinic. The designation is a gateway. Clinicians who agree to work at an approved site in a shortage area for at least two years can have student loans repaid through the
Attached to the designations is a second number,

. It is narrower than it sounds. The figure is the number of psychiatrists available in the designated areas divided by the number that would be needed to remove the designations, with the target set at one psychiatrist for every 30,000 people
. Only psychiatrists are counted. A county full of counselors and nurse practitioners and short of psychiatrists scores badly.
The third measure widens the lens.

's workforce ratio divides a state's population by all of its mental health providers: "psychiatrists, psychologists, licensed clinical social workers, counselors, marriage and family therapists, and advanced practice nurses"
. The fourth comes from inside the system. It is the count of funded posts that employers cannot fill.
The key idea in one picture

Draw four boxes in a column, each with a question on the left and Alabama's answer on the right. Box 1: "Where has the federal government recognized a shortage?" and "67 mental health shortage designations covering 2,934,202 people"
. Box 2: "Inside those areas, what share of the psychiatrists needed are there?" and "28.4 percent; psychiatrists only"
. Box 3: "Across the state, how many residents are there for each mental health provider of any kind?" and "740, against 320 nationally; ranked 51st
. Box 4: "In the public provider network, how many posts are empty?" and "752 of 4,678, at the end of
. Beside the column draw a two-step ladder labelled "
": the lower rung reads "state has joined", the upper rung "privileges are being issued here".
Alabama has 67 mental health shortage designations, and 2,934,202 people live in them, which is more than half the state's population of 5.19 million
. The count happens to equal the number of counties. Don't read it that way, since a designation can be a population group or a facility as easily as an area
Now the surprise. Alabama meets 28.4 percent of need in those areas, and the figure for the whole country, in the same federal data, is 27.3 percent
. On that measure Alabama looks unremarkable. Yet Mental Health America places the state 51st of 51 for
, with one provider for every 740 residents against one for every 320 nationally

. Both are right. Alabama's shortage areas are about as short of psychiatrists as shortage areas elsewhere, and the state has far fewer mental health professionals of all kinds, taken together, for its population. Anyone who quotes only the first number will understate the problem.

Neither figure says anything about the public system in particular. For that there is one data point. The Department reported in 2024 that its mental health provider network had 752 vacancies at the end of FY2023, against a need of 4,678 full-time positions
. No later statewide figure was found as of October 2026. The sharpest local case is the
, where about half of technician and nursing positions were filled in August 2024

Licensure compacts are the remedy most often mentioned, and they need the same careful reading. A compact lets a clinician licensed in one member state practice in another. Alabama has joined seven. The psychology compact has been in effect here since June 2021 and the nursing compact since January 2020
is a different story: ten states were issuing privileges under it by 1 October 2026, and Alabama was not yet one of them
. The Social Work compact, which Alabama joined in 2024, had not begun issuing multistate licenses anywhere
. Membership on paper adds no clinicians.
The longer-term remedy is training. The University of Alabama announced a
whose first class was to start in June 2026, with six residents a year
money to a psychiatry residency at UAB

Domain 4 gives all four measures in its first two paragraphs, so read them side by side there. Domain 7 adds the rural dimension, and Domain 4 itself notes that child psychiatry is the specialty most often named as short. The report's own reading is that the compacts and
end of the system and do nothing for inpatient units, which need staff on the ward
When a workforce number is quoted to you, ask which of the four it is, what year it describes and who is counted. The ranking is from data for 2024
. And Domain 4 is candid that on turnover and burnout Alabama publishes almost nothing at all.
